title: Season-Selective Rooftop Solar Collector Using an Asymmetric Non-Imaging Micro-Concentrator: Concept, Performance, and Independent Optical Check
content: Rooftop solar water heaters face a mismatch through the year. They collect the least heat in winter, when households need it most, and the most in summer, when the surplus overheats the system. This paper examines a collector, proposed by Chen et al., that tackles both problems passively. Rows of horizontal evacuated tubes sit on a 20° roof, each backed by a shallow, one-sided reflector shaped by the edge-ray method. When the sun’s projected altitude is below 50°, as it is in winter, the reflector concentrates light onto the tube. When the sun is higher, the reflected light misses the tube and returns to the sky. The 6 cm deep module showed a peak optical efficiency of 0.76, falling to about 0.35 at high sun. Outdoor tests gave daily efficiencies of 0.28–0.42, and the thermal model matched them with R2 = 0.985. Simulations for 371 Chinese cities reported 100–125% more winter heat than a flat-plate collector in cold northern regions and 4–26% less in summer. We reconstructed the reflector profile from the published equations and ray-traced it ourselves. Our curve, after a single loss factor of 0.83, reproduces both reported efficiency levels. A clear-sky seasonal analysis then shows that the reflectors raise winter beam capture by 1.5–1.7 times over bare tubes and leave summer capture unchanged. On beam optics alone, however, the module does not out-collect a flat plate in winter, so most of its winter advantage comes from the low heat loss of the evacuated tubes. We also note inconsistencies in the reported payback and seasonal figures.
